title: Qurrium: A Python package for randomized measurement-based estimation of quantum state properties
authors: Huai-Chun Chang, Teik-Hui Lee, Arthur Strauss, Yu-Cheng Lin, Hsiu-Chuan Hsu
abstract: Estimating quantum state properties is essential across a wide range of applications, from studying quantum many-body physics to benchmarking quantum hardware. We present Qurrium, a Python package built on Qiskit that implements randomized measurement protocols for estimating purity, second-order Rényi entropy, expectation values of Pauli observables, and state overlap. In this paper, we focus on the classical shadow protocol and demonstrate two workflows in Qurrium. One is the end-to-end workflow that integrates quantum circuit preparation, simulation, measurement, and analysis. The other is the standalone estimation workflow that accepts pre-collected measurement data from any hardware platform in Qurrium's data format. We demonstrate both workflows through examples of a cluster state and an Ising time-evolved state. Furthermore, we report results obtained from a superconducting quantum processor developed by Academia Sinica and analyzed using the standalone estimation workflow. Qurrium is built on Qiskit, the dominant framework in quantum computing software, making it directly accessible to the large community of researchers already working with Qiskit. The source code is openly available at https://github.com/qurrium/qurrium and the example code is provided at https://github.com/qurrium/classical-shadow-examples.
summary: This paper presents Qurrium, a Python package built on Qiskit, designed to estimate quantum state properties efficiently using randomized measurement protocols like the classical shadow protocol. It offers two workflows—one for simulation and one for analyzing raw hardware data—allowing researchers to characterize complex states like cluster states and measure observables on real quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the essential need to estimate quantum state properties (like purity, entropy, and overlaps) without performing full quantum state tomography.
main_result: It introduces Qurrium, a Python package built on Qiskit, that implements randomized measurement protocols, specifically the classical shadow protocol, for efficient state characterization.
method: The methodology centers on using randomized measurements (classical shadow protocol) to estimate expectation values and state properties, demonstrated through both end-to-end simulation workflows and standalone analysis of hardware-collected data.
model_or_system: The package is tested on theoretical models like the cluster state and Ising time-evolved states, and validated using measurements from a superconducting quantum processor.
key_observables: Purity ($	ext{Tr}(ho^2)$), second-order Rényi entropy ($S^{(2)}(ho)$), expectation values of Pauli observables ($\langle O angle$), and state overlaps ($	ext{Tr}(hoho')$).
important_parameters: The analysis depends on the structure of the quantum state (e.g., cluster state stabilizers) and the separation distance ($d$) between subsystems.
main_assumptions: The standalone workflow assumes measurement outcomes and random unitaries are recorded in the specific Qurrium data format; the efficiency gains are implementation-level and do not change statistical complexity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the end-to-end and standalone workflows. Specific results show the overlap between the cluster state and reference states, and the decay of mutual information $I^{(2)}(A:B)$ with separation distance $d$.
paper_structure: The paper reviews the classical shadow protocol, details the two distinct workflows within Qurrium (end-to-end and standalone), and then demonstrates usage with concrete examples like the cluster state and Ising dynamics.
why_interesting: For AMO physicists studying open quantum systems, this provides a crucial, hardware-agnostic tool to characterize complex quantum states (like those generated by cavity QED or trapped ions) using measurement data, bypassing the need for full tomography.
